{{Short description|Nondimensional heat transfer coefficient}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2020}}

The '''Nusselt number''' is a nondimensionalization of the convective [[heat transfer coefficient]]. Like the heat transfer coefficient, the Nusselt number may be defined locally, at a single position on a surface, or as an average value that represents the heat flow from the entire surface.

The Nusselt number is named in honor of [[Wilhelm Nusselt]], who first identified this dimensionless group in 1915.

Analytical results and empirical correlations allow the Nusselt number to be estimated in many situations. For [[forced convection]], these expressions depend on the [[Reynolds number]] and the [[Prandtl number]]. For [[natural convection]] (or "free" convection) the predictions use the [[Grashof number]] or [[Rayleigh number]] along with the Prandtl number.

The [[mass transfer]] analog of the Nusselt number is the [[Sherwood number]].

== History ==
[[File:Bewerbungs foto BASF Prof Nusselt Anufuahme von Januar 1916.jpg|upright=1.2|thumb|Wilhelm Nusselt in January 1916|alt=photo of Wilhelm Nusselt in January 1916]]
The group now known as the Nusselt number was first identified by [[Wilhelm Nusselt]] in a 1915 paper.<ref name="Nusselt1915">{{cite journal|last = Nusselt|first = Wilhelm|author-link=Wilhelm Nusselt|date = 1915|title = Das Grundgesetz des Wärmeüberganges|journal = Gesundheits-Ingenieur|volume = 38|issue = 42–43|pages = 477–482, 490–496|language = de|translator-last1 = Wachmann|translator-first1 =C.| translator-last2 =Brown|translator-first2 =W. G.|publisher = National Research Council of Canada|publication-date = 1957|url = https://nrc-publications.canada.ca/eng/view/fulltext/?id=36494c75-ac61-4b40-b5cc-12fb6484532b}}</ref><ref name="schmidt">{{cite journal |last=Schmidt |first=E. |title=Wilhelm Nusselt |journal=Zeitschrift des Vereins Deutscher Ingenieure |volume=99 |pages=1741–1742 |year=1957|language=de |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2027/uc1.c2607909?urlappend=%3Bseq%3D437%3Bownerid%3D120557628-503}}</ref>  In that paper, he also identified the groups that became the Grashof number, the Prandtl number, and the Reynolds number.<ref name="kling">{{cite journal |last=Kling |first=G. |title=Aus der Entwicklungsgeschichte der Wärmeübergangslehre: Wilhelm Nußelt zum 70. Geburtstag |journal=Chemie Ingenieur Technik |volume=24 |pages=597–608 |year=1952 |doi=10.1002/cite.330241102 |language=de}}</ref> Nusselt used these groups effectively to correlate data for natural convection and, in a 1917 paper, forced convection.<ref name="Nusselt1915"/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Nusselt|first=Wilhelm|year=1917|title=Der Wärmeübergang im Rohr|journal=Zeitschrift des Vereines Deutscher Ingenieure|volume=61|pages=685–689|language=de|url=https://archive.org/details/zeitschrift-des-vereines-deutscher-ingenieure-61.1917-teil-2}}</ref> 

In 1931, the [[Verein Deutscher Ingenieure|Association of German Engineers]] formally named the dimensionless group the ''Nusselt number''.<ref name="schmidt"/> The decision was announced in paper by [[Max Jakob]].<ref name="jakob">{{cite journal
|last=Jakob
|first=M.
|author-link=Max Jakob
|date=25 July 1931
|title=Fortschritte der Wärmeforschung im Verein deutscher Ingenieure
|trans-title=Advances in Heat Research within the Association of German Engineers
|journal=Zeitschrift des Vereines Deutscher Ingenieure
|volume=75
|issue=30
|pages=969–971
|language=de
}} Contains S. Erk, "Die Grundgedanken der Theorien des Wärmeüberganges" [The Fundamental Concepts of the Theories of Heat Transfer], p. 970.</ref> The term was quickly adopted internationally.<ref name="colburn">{{cite journal|last=Colburn|first=Allan P.|year=1933|title=A method of correlating forced convection heat-transfer data and a comparison with fluid friction|journal=Transactions of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers|volume=29|pages=174–206}}</ref>

== Definition ==
The heat transfer coefficient, <math>h</math>, at a surface cooled by a fluid is the ratio of the [[heat flux]] <math>q</math> [W/m<sup>2</sup>] from the surface to the temperature difference <math>\Delta T</math> [K]
between the surface and the fluid far from the surface: <math>h = q/\Delta T</math> [W/(m<sup>2</sup>·K)]. The Nusselt number, <math>\textrm{Nu}</math>, is formed by nondimensionalizing <math>h</math> with a [[characteristic length]] <math>L</math> [m] and the [[thermal conductivity]] of the fluid <math>k</math> [W/(m·K)]:{{r|lienhard|p=298–299}}
:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_L = \frac{qL}{k\Delta T}  = \frac{hL}{k}</math>

The Nusselt number is a [[dimensionless number|dimensionless group]]. The subscript, ''L'', indicates which characteristic length is used.
 
=== Selection of characteristic length ===
The characteristic length should be related to the thickness of the thermal [[boundary layer]]. In a tube, the thermal boundary layer will be limited by the tube diameter, <math>D</math>, so that the diameter represents the scale of the boundary layer. On a flat plate, the length of the plate, <math>L</math>, determines the average thickness of the boundary layer on the plate.  On the other hand, the local thickness of the flat plate boundary layer, at a position <math>x</math>, is determined by the value of <math>x</math>, so that <math>x</math> is the characteristic length for the local heat transfer coefficient on the plate.{{r|lienhard}}

Some additional examples of characteristic length are: the outer diameter of a cylinder in (external) crossflow (perpendicular to the cylinder axis), the height of a vertical plate undergoing [[natural convection]], or the diameter of a sphere. For complex shapes, the length may be defined as the volume of the fluid body divided by the surface area.{{r|lienhard}}

=== Local and average Nusselt numbers ===
At a location <math>x</math> on a surface, the local heat transfer coefficient, <math>h_x</math>, relates the local heat flux, <math>q</math>, to the local temperature difference <math>\Delta T_x</math>:
:<math>q = h_x \Delta T_x</math>
The local heat transfer coefficient varies along the surface of a body. It becomes lower as the thermal boundary layer becomes thicker. It increases suddenly where the boundary layer transitions from laminar to turbulent flow.

The local Nusselt number is a nondimensionalization of the local heat transfer coefficient, <math>h_x </math>, at a position <math>x</math> on a surface:
:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_x = \frac{h_x x}{k}</math>

The average heat transfer coefficient relates the average temperature difference to the average heat flux over the body. For an ''isothermal'' body the temperature difference is constant, and if the body has length <math>L</math> the average heat flux is{{r|lienhard|p=308–309}}
:<math>\overline{q}=\frac{1}{L} \int_0^L q_x \ dx = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L h_x \Delta T\ dx = \frac{\Delta T}{L} \int_0^L h_x \ dx = \overline{h} \Delta T</math>
The ''average'' Nusselt number is then defined as
:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L = \frac{\overline{h}L}{k}</math>

For a uniform flux surface, the temperature difference is not constant, and so the temperature difference must be averaged to find the average heat transfer coefficient:{{r|lienhard|p=311–312}}
:<math> q = \overline{h} \times \overline{\Delta T}</math>
The average temperature difference is another integral:
:<math>\overline{\Delta T}=\frac{1}{L} \int_0^L \frac{q}{h_x} \ dx = \frac{q}{L} \int_0^L \frac{1}{h_x}\ dx </math>
The average Nusselt number is defined just as for an isothermal surface:
:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L = \frac{\overline{h}L}{k}</math>

The term "average Nusselt number" can cause confusion because the Nusselt number is not what has been averaged. For an isothermal surface, the heat flux has been averaged, while for a uniform flux surface, the temperature difference has been averaged.

=== Stanton number===
A closely related dimensionless group is the [[Stanton number]] used in some studies of forced convection:
:<math>\textrm{St} = \frac{\textrm{Nu}}{\textrm{Re Pr}} = \frac{h}{\rho c_p u}</math>
where <math> \rho, c_p, \text{and } u</math> are the fluid [[density]], [[specific heat capacity]], and free stream speed.{{r|lienhard|p=313}}

=== Confusion with the Biot number ===
A similar nondimensional group is the [[Biot number]], which compares the thermal resistance of heat conduction in the body to the thermal resistance of convection outside the body. The Biot number uses the thermal conductivity of the solid body rather than the fluid.{{r|lienhard|p=21–26}} The Biot number should not be confused with the Nusselt number.

== Relationship of Nusselt number to laminar boundary layer thickness ==
An understanding of convection boundary layers is necessary to understand convective heat transfer between a surface and a fluid flowing past it. A thermal boundary layer develops if the fluid free stream temperature and the surface temperatures differ. A temperature profile is created by the energy exchange resulting from this temperature difference. [[File:Thermal Boundary Layer Thickness formed by heated fluid flow along a plate.jpg|upright=2.5|thumb|Thermal and momentum boundary layers for laminar flow past a flat plate. The thermal boundary layer thickness, ''δ<sub>t</sub>'', is the lower dashed curve.|alt=Sketch of momentum and thermal boundary layers in laminar flat-plate flow, including temperature and velocity profiles]]

The local heat transfer rate can be written using [[Newton's law of cooling]] as
:<math>q=h_x\left( T_s-T_0 \right)</math>
At the surface of the body, the fluid velocity is zero as a result of the [[no-slip condition]], so heat transfer in the fluid at the surface is by conduction alone:
:<math>q=-k\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left. \left( T-T_s \right) \right|_{y=0}</math>.

These two terms are equal; thus{{r|lienhard|p=276–277}}
:<math>h_x = -\frac{k}{\left( T_s-T_0 \right)}\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left. \left( T-T_s \right) \right|_{y=0}</math>.

For a laminar boundary layer (see figure), the temperature gradient at the surface has a temperature change <math>T_s-T_0</math> over a distance proportional to the thermal boundary layer thickness, <math>\delta_t</math>, so a crude approximation is:
:<math>-\frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left. \left( T-T_s \right) \right|_{y=0}\approx \frac{T_s-T_0}{\delta_t} </math>.
Hence, the laminar Nusselt number is greater when the thermal boundary layer is thinner:{{r|lienhard|p=276–277}}
:<math>\textrm{Nu}_x =\frac{h_x x}{k} \approx \frac{x}{\delta_t} </math>

==Analytical results and empirical correlations for Nu==
For forced convection, the Nusselt number is generally a function of the [[Reynolds number]] and the [[Prandtl number]], or{{r|lienhard|p=299}}

:<math>\mathrm{Nu} = f(\mathrm{Re}, \mathrm{Pr})</math>

For free, or natural, convection, the average Nusselt number is usually expressed as a function of the [[Rayleigh number]] or [[Grashof number]] and the [[Prandtl number]]:{{r|lienhard|p=417–419}}

:<math>\mathrm{Nu} = f(\mathrm{Ra}, \mathrm{Pr})</math>
or
:<math>\mathrm{Nu} = f(\mathrm{Gr}, \mathrm{Pr})</math>
since Ra = GrPr.

Analytical results and empirical correlations  that express the Nusselt number in the aforementioned forms are available for a wide variety of geometries.

=== Evaluation of physical properties ===
When calculating the Nusselt number, the thermal conductivity, the [[Prandtl number]], and the properties in the [[Reynolds number| Reynolds]] or [[Grashof number]]s are usually evaluated at the [[film temperature]]. The film temperature is the average of the wall temperature and free stream or bulk temperature.{{r|lienhard|p=310}} When the bulk temperature changes significantly along the length of the tube, the average bulk temperature can be used.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}}

== Free, or natural, convection ==

=== Free convection at a vertical wall ===
Churchill and Chu correlated a wide range of data with the following expression, which includes both laminar and turbulent flow:<ref name="ChurchillChu1975">{{cite journal |last1=Churchill |first1=S. W. |last2=Chu |first2=H. H. S. |title=Correlating equations for laminar and turbulent free convection from a vertical plate |journal=International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer |volume=18 |issue=11 |pages=1323–1329 |date=November 1975 |doi=10.1016/0017-9310(75)90243-4}}</ref>

:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = \left({0.825 + \frac{0.387 \mathrm{Ra}_L^{1/6}}{\left(1 + (0.492/\mathrm{Pr})^{9/16} \right)^{8/27} }}\right)^2 \, \quad \mathrm{Ra}_L < 10^{12}</math>

The transition from a laminar to a turbulent boundary occurs at <math>\mathrm{Ra}_L \approx 10^9 </math>. For laminar flows, Churchill and Chu recommended the following, slightly more accurate correlation:
:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = 0.68 + \frac{0.67 \mathrm{Ra}_L^{1/4}}{\left(1 + (0.492/\mathrm{Pr})^{9/16}\right)^{4/9}} \, \quad 10^{-1} < \mathrm{Ra}_L < 10^9 </math>

=== Free convection from horizontal plates ===
If the characteristic length is defined

:<math>L \ = \frac{A_s}{P}</math>

where <math>\mathrm{A}_s</math> is the surface area of the plate and <math>P</math> is its perimeter.

Then for the top surface of a hot object in a colder environment or bottom surface of a cold object in a hotter environment{{r|incropera|p=577}}

:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = 0.54\, \mathrm{Ra}_L^{1/4} \, \quad 10^4 \le \mathrm{Ra}_L \le 10^7</math>

:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = 0.15\, \mathrm{Ra}_L^{1/3} \, \quad 10^7 \le \mathrm{Ra}_L \le 10^{11}</math>

And for the bottom surface of a hot object in a colder environment or top surface of a cold object in a hotter environment{{r|incropera|p=577}}

:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = 0.27\, \mathrm{Ra}_L^{1/4} \, \quad 10^5 \le \mathrm{Ra}_L \le 10^{10}</math>

=== Free convection from enclosure heated from below ===
In 1959, Globe and Dropkin reported the following correlation for wide fluid layers between a lower heated and upper cooled plate:<ref name="globe">{{Cite journal |last1=Globe |first1=Samuel |last2=Dropkin |first2=David |date=1959 |title=Natural-Convection Heat Transfer in Liquids Confined by Two Horizontal Plates and Heated From Below |url=https://asmedigitalcollection.asme.org/heattransfer/article-abstract/81/1/24/397579/Natural-Convection-Heat-Transfer-in-Liquids?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Journal of Heat Transfer |volume=81 |issue=1 |pages=24–28 |doi=10.1115/1.4008124 |via=ASME Digital Collection|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = 0.069\, \mathrm{Ra}_L^{1/3}\mathrm{Pr}^{0.074} \, \quad 1.5 \times 10^5 \le \mathrm{Ra}_L \le 6.8 \times 10^{8} \;\text{and}\; 0.02 \le \mathrm{Pr} \le 8750 </math>

This equation ''"holds when the horizontal layer is sufficiently wide so that the effect of the short vertical sides is minimal."''<ref name="globe" />

== Forced convection ==
===Flat plate in laminar flow===
The solution of the energy and [[Blasius boundary layer|momentum equations]] for laminar flow over an isothermal flat plate leads to the following equation for the local Nusselt number at a distance <math>x</math> downstream from the leading edge of the plate.{{r|incropera|p=490}}

:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_x\ = 0.332\, \mathrm{Re}_x^{1/2}\, \mathrm{Pr}^{1/3},\quad \mathrm{Pr} > 0.6 </math>

The average Nusselt number for laminar flow over an isothermal flat plate, from the edge of the plate to a downstream distance <math>L</math>, is given by{{r|incropera|p=490}}

:<math>\overline{\mathrm{Nu}}_L \ = {2} \cdot 0.332\, \mathrm{Re}_L^{1/2}\, \mathrm{Pr}^{1/3}\ = 0.664\, \mathrm{Re}_L^{1/2}\, \mathrm{Pr}^{1/3}, \quad \mathrm{Pr} > 0.6 </math>

===Sphere in forced flow===
For a sphere in forced flow, such as an evaporating droplet, Faeth suggests:<ref name="Faeth1977">{{cite journal |last=Faeth |first=G. M. |title=Current status of droplet and liquid combustion |journal=Progress in Energy and Combustion Science |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=191–224 |year=1977 |doi=10.1016/0360-1285(77)90012-0}}</ref>

:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_D \ = {2} + \frac{0.555\, \mathrm{Re}_D^{1/2}\, \mathrm{Pr}^{1/3}}{\left(1+ 1.232/(\mathrm{Re} \mathrm{Pr}^{4/3})\right)^{1/2}}, \quad \mathrm{Re}_D< 1800 </math>
The result limits to <math>\mathrm{Nu}_D \ = {2}</math> for small Reynolds numbers, which corresponds to heat conduction into a sphere in an infinite medium.{{r|lienhard|p=433}}

===Forced convection in turbulent pipe flow===

====Gnielinski correlation====
Gnielinski's correlation (1975) for flow in smooth tubes is:<ref name="Gnielinski1975">{{cite journal |last=Gnielinski |first=Volker |title=Neue Gleichungen für den Wärme- und den Stoffübergang in turbulent durchströmten Rohren und Kanälen |pages=8–16 |year=1975 |journal=Forsch. Ing.-Wes. |volume=41 |issue=1|doi=10.1007/BF02559682 |s2cid=124105274 }}</ref><ref name="incropera">{{cite book |author-link=Frank P. Incropera |last1=Incropera |first1=Frank P. |last2=DeWitt |first2=David P. |title=Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsheat00incr_617 |url-access=limited |edition=6th |location=Hoboken |publisher=Wiley |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-471-45728-2 }}</ref>{{rp|pp=490,515}}
:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_D = \frac{ \left( f/8 \right) \left( \mathrm{Re}_D - 1000 \right) \mathrm{Pr} } {1 + 12.7(f/8)^{1/2} \left( \mathrm{Pr}^{2/3} - 1 \right)}</math>

where <math>f</math> is the [[Darcy friction factor]] that can either be obtained from the [[Moody chart]] or from the correlation of Filonenko:<ref name="filonenko1954">{{cite journal|last=Filonenko|first=G. K.|script-title=ru:Гидравлическое сопротивление в трубах|trans-title=Hydraulic resistance in pipes|language=ru|journal=Teploenergetika|volume=1|issue=4|pages=40–44|year=1954}}</ref>
:<math>f= \left( 0.79 \ln \left(\mathrm{Re}_D \right)-1.64 \right)^{-2}</math>

The Gnielinski correlation is valid for:{{r|incropera|p=490}}

:<math>0.5 \le \mathrm{Pr} \le 2000</math>
:<math>3000 \le \mathrm{Re}_D \le 5 \times 10^{6}</math>

This correlation is much more accurate than 1930s power-law correlations such as the Dittus–Boelter equation.<ref name="lienhard">{{Cite book|last1=Lienhard IV|first1=John Henry|last2=Lienhard V|first2=John Henry|title=A Heat Transfer Textbook|date=2024|publisher=Phlogiston Press|edition=6th|location=Cambridge, MA|url=https://ahtt.mit.edu}}</ref>{{rp|pp=368–371}}

==== Gnielinski's simplified correlations ====
Gnielinski also developed power-law correlations for limited ranges of Prandtl number, which agree very closely with his full-range correlation.  These equations are simpler to use, while remaining accurate:{{r|Gnielinski1975}}{{r|lienhard|p=371}}
:<math>\begin{aligned}
\textrm{Nu}_D &= 0.0214 \left( \textrm{Re}^{0.8}_D -100 \right)\textrm{Pr}^{0.4} &\quad&\textrm{for} \quad 0.6\le \textrm{Pr}\le 1.5 \\
\textrm{Nu}_D & = 0.012 \left( \textrm{Re}^{0.87}_D -280 \right)\textrm{Pr}^{0.4} &\quad&\textrm{for} \quad 1.5 \le \textrm{Pr}\le 500
\end{aligned}</math>
These equations apply for smooth tubes with <math>3000 \le \mathrm{Re}_D \le 5 \times 10^{6}</math>.

====Dittus–Boelter equation====
The Dittus–Boelter equation (for turbulent flow in smooth-walled tubes), as introduced by W.H. McAdams,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Winterton |first1=R.H.S. |title=Where did the Dittus and Boelter equation come from? |journal=International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer |date=February 1998 |volume=41 |issue=4–5 |pages=809–810 |doi=10.1016/S0017-9310(97)00177-4 |publisher=Elsevier|bibcode=1998IJHMT..41..809W |url=http://herve.lemonnier.sci.free.fr/TPF/NE/Winterton.pdf}}</ref> is one of several power-law correlations that were published in the 1930s.{{r|lienhard|p=368–371}}  These equations are based on smaller data sets than the Gnielinski correlations, represent smaller ranges of Reynolds and Prandtl number, and are generally less accurate.{{r|lienhard|p=368–371}} The Dittus–Boelter equation is:

:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_D = 0.023\, \mathrm{Re}_D^{4/5}\, \mathrm{Pr}^{n}</math>

where:
:<math>D</math> is the inside diameter of the circular duct
:<math>\mathrm{Pr}</math> is the [[Prandtl number]]
:<math>n = 0.4</math> for the fluid being heated, and <math>n = 0.3</math> for the fluid being cooled.{{r|incropera|p=493}}

The Dittus–Boelter equation is valid for{{r|incropera|p=514}}
:<math>0.6 \le \mathrm{Pr} \le 160</math>
:<math>\mathrm{Re}_D \gtrsim 10\,000</math>
:<math>\frac{L}{D} \gtrsim 10</math>

==== Sieder–Tate correlation ====
The Sieder–Tate correlation for turbulent pipe flow (1936) takes account of the change in [[viscosity]] (<math>\mu_b</math> and <math>\mu_w</math>) due to temperature change between the average bulk temperature of the fluid and wall temperature. The Sieder–Tate correlation may need to be solved iteratively if the bulk or wall temperature is unknown.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sieder|first1=E. N.|last2=Tate|first2=G. E.|year=1936|title=Heat transfer and pressure drop of liquids in tubes|journal=Industrial & Engineering Chemistry|volume=28|issue=12|pages=1429–1435|doi=10.1021/ie50324a027}}</ref>

:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_D = 0.027\,\mathrm{Re}_D^{4/5}\, \mathrm{Pr}^{1/3}\left(\frac{\mu_b}{\mu_w}\right)^{0.14}</math>
where:
:<math>\mu_b</math> is the fluid viscosity at the bulk fluid temperature
:<math>\mu_w</math> is the fluid viscosity at tube wall

The Sieder–Tate correlation is valid for{{r|incropera|p=493}}

:<math>0.7 \le \mathrm{Pr} \le 16\,700</math>
:<math>\mathrm{Re}_D \ge 10\,000</math>
:<math>\frac{L}{D} \gtrsim 10</math>

Taking water with a bulk fluid average temperature of {{cvt|20|C}}, viscosity {{val|10.07e-4|u=Pa.s}} and a heat transfer surface temperature of {{cvt|40|C}} (viscosity {{val|6.96e-4|u=Pa.s}}, a viscosity correction factor for <math>({\mu} / {\mu_s})</math> can be obtained as 1.45. This increases to 3.57 with a heat transfer surface temperature of {{cvt|100|C}} (viscosity {{val|2.82e-4|u=Pa.s}}), making a significant difference to the Nusselt number and the heat transfer coefficient.

=== Forced convection in fully developed laminar flow in a tube ===
Solution of the governing equations for fully developed, laminar pipe flow leads to very simple results. The Nusselt numbers tend towards a constant value for long tubes:
:<math>\mathrm{Nu} = \frac{h D_h}{k}</math>
where:

:''D<sub>h</sub>'' = [[hydraulic diameter]]
:''k'' = [[thermal conductivity]] of the fluid
:''h'' = [[convective]] [[heat transfer coefficient]]

====Convection with uniform wall temperature for circular tubes====
From Incropera & DeWitt,{{r|incropera|pp=486–487}}

:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_D = 3.66</math>

OEIS sequence {{OEIS link|A282581}} gives this value as <math>\mathrm{Nu}_D = 3.6567934577632923619...</math>.

====Convection with uniform wall heat flux for circular tubes====
For the case of constant surface heat flux,{{r|incropera|pp=486–487}}

:<math>\mathrm{Nu}_D = 4.36</math>
